rationale: Evidence across cohort and proband studies confirms that seizures (e.g., absence, tonic) and hypotonia occur recurrently in individuals with pathogenic LRRC7 variants (including 6/33 individuals with seizures in Willim et al. 2024, along with proband reports in Popp et al. 2017 and Khan et al. 2026). Because both seizures and muscular hypotonia can be present in LRRC7-related disorder (OMIM #621415), the presence of these features cannot rule out LRRC7 when evaluating a differential diagnosis against other postsynaptic scaffolding synaptopathies such as SYNGAP1, SHANK3, or DLG4, and their absence similarly cannot reliably exclude LRRC7 since neither is fully penetrant.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 33 individuals with heterozygous missense or loss-of-function variants in LRRC7, varying types of seizures were reported in six patients, demonstrating that seizures are part of the phenotypic spectrum rather than an exclusionary feature.

new_directions.question_text: What is the precise semiology, age of onset, and EEG signature of seizures in LRRC7-related disorder compared to SYNGAP1-related encephalopathy?
new_directions.rationale: While seizures occur in LRRC7 (~18-20% in published series), SYNGAP1 exhibits much higher penetrance (>80%) often with eyelid myoclonia and atonic/myoclonic seizures; detailed electroclinical profiling could clarify whether specific seizure types discriminate between these synaptopathies.

new_directions.question_text: Do behavioral profiles—specifically hyperphagia/abnormal eating behaviors and severe aggression—provide sufficient specificity to distinguish LRRC7 variants from SHANK3 or DLG4 variants?
new_directions.rationale: Willim et al. noted prominent aggression, hyperphagia, and abnormal eating patterns as core discriminating behavioral manifestations of LRRC7, which may serve as superior positive discriminators than non-specific neurological findings like hypotonia.
